title: Introduction to Two Pointers
description: Understand how using two pointers can reduce time complexity and simplify array and string problems

blocks.text: A simple pattern that uses two index variables instead of one and turns many O(n²) problems into clean O(n) solutions.

Instead of using a single loop index, you keep two pointers usually called left and right and move them based on a condition. This lets you look at two positions in the array at the same time without nested loops.
When to use it:The array is sorted, or the problem involves comparing elements from two different positions like checking pairs, reversals, or merging.
Left starts at index 0, right starts at the last index. They move toward each other until they meet. Used for pair-sum problems, palindrome checks, and reversals.
Example: pair that sums to a target
Array: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]  |  Target: 12
Step 1: left=0 (1), right=5 (11). Sum = 12 ✓ found!

blocks.alt: Opposite ends two pointer finding a pair that sums to target

blocks.text: Left=0, right=5 | 1+11=12 |found the pair!
But what if the sum is too small or too big? Here's how the pointers move:
If sum < target move left forward (need a bigger number)
sum too small →move left →
If sum > target move right backward (need a smaller number)
sum too big →← move right
two sum on sorted array
Both pointers start at the left and move in the same direction. One pointer (slow) marks a position, the other (fast) scans ahead. Used for removing duplicates, partitioning, or merging.
Example:  remove duplicates from sorted array
Array: [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4] keep only unique values in-place.
slow tracks where the next unique value goes. fast scans for the next new value.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785250770164-514252354.png
blocks.alt: Slow and fast pointer removing duplicates, step 1

blocks.text: slow=0, fast=1 | arr[fast]==arr[slow] →skip, move fast →
slow=0, fast=2 | arr[fast]!=arr[slow] →write 2, move slow →
slow=1, fast=3 | arr[fast]!=arr[slow] →write 3, move slow →
slow=2, fast=4 | arr[fast]==arr[slow] →skip, move fast →
slow=2, fast=5 | arr[fast]!=arr[slow] →write 4 → done!
Result: first 4 slots = [1, 2, 3, 4] all duplicates removed.
The Template

items: Is the array sorted? Opposite-ends two pointer only works on sorted arrays. Same-direction works on both.
Set your pointers. Opposite ends:left=0, right=n-1. Same direction:slow=0, fast=1.
Loop while left < right(opposite ends) or while fast < n(same direction).
Move the right pointer when you need a smaller value, move left when you need a bigger one or move fast when values match.

blocks.text: Where You'll See This

items: Two sum / three sum on a sorted array
Check if a string is a palindrome
Remove duplicates from a sorted array
Move all zeros to the end
Reverse an array or string in-place

blocks.text: Remember: Two pointer works best on sorted arrays for opposite-ends problems. If the array is unsorted and you need pairs, consider using a hash map instead that's O(n) without sorting.
